verses.text: Yahweh says, “Maintain justice, and do what is right; for my salvation is near, and my righteousness will soon be revealed.
Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast; who keeps the Sabbath without profaning it, and keeps his hand from doing any evil.”
Let no foreigner, who has joined himself to Yahweh, speak, saying, “Yahweh will surely separate me from his people.” Do not let the eunuch say, “Behold, I am a dry tree.”
For Yahweh says, “To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, and choose the things that please me, and hold fast to my covenant:
I will give them in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than of sons and of daughters. I will give them an everlasting name, that will not be cut off.
Also the foreigners who join themselves to Yahweh, to serve him, and to love Yahweh’s name, to be his servants, everyone who keeps the Sabbath from profaning it, and holds fast my covenant;

I will bring these to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be accepted on my altar; for my house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples.”
The Lord Yahweh, who gathers the outcasts of Israel, says, “I will yet gather others to him, besides his own who are gathered.”
All you animals of the field, come to devour, all you animals in the forest.
His watchmen are blind. They are all without knowledge. They are all mute dogs. They can’t bark; dreaming, lying down, loving to slumber.
Yes, the dogs are greedy. They can never have enough. They are shepherds who can’t understand. They have all turned to their own way, each one to his gain, from every quarter.
“Come,” say they, “I will get wine, and we will fill ourselves with strong drink; and tomorrow will be as today, great beyond measure.”

footnotes.content: The Lord's mercy doesn't ask us to wait for a better day—it's already near. What a tender word to people worn down by exile and loss. We do justice and righteousness not to earn salvation, but because we're swept up in something God is already doing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Sabbath is no burden here—it's a sign of someone who has decided to belong to the Lord's rhythm instead of the world's demands. 'Blessed is' the man, not because he never stumbles, but because he knows what he's holding onto.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The foreigner and the eunuch—both lived outside the old covenant's full promises. Here Isaiah names the very people whom ancient law had left uncertain, and God Himself says: you are not forsaken. The Lord's house is bigger than our categories.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God speaks directly to the eunuchs, as if to say: I see you. I know what you've lost. And I'm making a covenant with you—not a side covenant, not a watered-down one. The same covenant, kept with the same care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An everlasting name means belonging that cannot be erased or forgotten. In a world that had made them invisible, God offers not just inclusion but honor—a name written in His house forever. That's how He heals what the world has broken.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The foreigners who love the Lord's name and keep His covenant are not converts to an ethnic group—they're joining themselves to the God of Israel. Love and faithfulness are what make you family at His table.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: My house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples—here is the whole vision drawn in one line. The temple, the mountain, the altar are open to the unlikely and the far-off. Jesus would echo this when He made the same space welcoming to all who sought the Father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord gathers the outcasts of Israel, and then says He will gather more—as if mercy's work is never finished, never satisfied until all who are far off are brought in. That generous heart is who God is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The tone shifts hard here. The wild animals come to feed—a sign that the shepherds have failed and the flock is left unguarded. Isaiah turns now to call out the blindness of those who should have been watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The watchmen are blind, the dogs cannot bark—they've fallen asleep on the job. Sometimes faithlessness looks like slumber, not rebellion. We drift away from what we're meant to guard, and don't even notice we've stopped watching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Greedy dogs who can never have enough, shepherds turned toward their own gain—this is the dark mirror to verses 1-8. Where the faithful do justice and keep covenant, the leaders pursue only themselves. Each one to his own way: the opposite of the Lord's mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Come, they say, let's drink and tomorrow will be just like today—readers today hear an echo in that empty promise. We still hear it in voices that say there's no cost to living for ourselves, that tomorrow will be fine. The Lord knew we'd need this warning still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
